schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch frame the three chapters as one whole of worship led by Ezra, the seventh month opening with the feast of trumpets; Ellicott stresses that 'as one man' emphasizes unanimity not number, and that Ezra reappears after twelve years at the Persian court.

Henry weighs every circumstance — the day (Lev. 23:24; Num. 29:1) when the altar had been set up, the spacious street before the temple, the whole people met voluntarily as one man, and Ezra the ready scribe called by the people to bring the book.
Gill hears in the gathering 'as one man' great unanimity, zeal, and affection.
Clarke locates the water gate as the gate leading from the temple to the brook Kidron.

themes: Ezra called to read the law

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch describe the six-hour reading from early morning, broken by Levitical exposition; Ellicott defines the hearers as men, women, and children of years of discretion, the first day being the year's most important new moon (Lev. 23:24).

Clarke excludes infants yet pleads that a poor mother not be barred with her child in arms; Wesley fixes the feast of trumpets, a sabbath and holy convocation (Lev. 23:24), on which the altar had been set up after the captivity.
Gill notes the perfect, well-known copy Ezra produced, though some restrict the reading to Deuteronomy.

themes: the law brought before the congregation
the reading from morning to midday
the first day of the seventh month

schools.summary: Ellicott renders 'from the morning' as from daylight and infers a comprehensive book read selectively hour after hour; Keil and Delitzsch fix about six hours, the reading alternating with Levitical lectures, the people listening attentively.
Gill: Ezra read not in order but selected passages the people most needed to know.
Henry makes attentive hearing the heart of the verse — the ears of all chained to the book for six hours, for the word commands attention, and carelessness in hearing risks forgetfulness after.
Gill glosses the Hebrew 'tower' as named for height, form, and largeness, broad enough for fourteen men, likening it to the king's platform and the later synagogue desk (Aben Ezra).
Clarke hails the migdal as the first intimation of a pulpit, raised to lift the reader above the people, and jibes that it was nothing like the confining tubs of his own day's churches.

Keil and Delitzsch describe the raised stage, six on the right and seven on the left, and judge a name (Azariah) dropped by clerical slip since the Greek Esdras balances the sides; Ellicott reads 'a tower of wood' with fourteen persons on the platform beside Ezra.

Keil and Delitzsch note Ezra 'above all the people,' the opening of the book in their sight, and the whole congregation rising — cautioning that standing at the reading cannot be proved a Mosaic custom as the Rabbis assert.
Clarke reads the people's rising as respect for the sacred word, the origin of the Christian usage of standing for the gospel.
Gill: Ezra so placed that all could see and hear, the pulpit made for the purpose.
Henry dwells on the reverence of the opening — no longer a fountain sealed — urging solemn stops and pauses in the services of religion (Eccl. 5:1), servants standing when the master speaks.

outliers.note: Caution that standing at the reading of the law cannot be shown from the Old Testament to be a Mosaic custom, contrary to the Rabbinic assertion (citing Vitringa).

themes: the origin of a church usage

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch take the blessing as perhaps a thanksgiving like David's (1 Chron. 29:10), answered by a double Amen (1 Chron. 16:36) with lifted hands and faces to the ground; Ellicott traces the same double gesture of assent and adoration.
Gill: a short benedictory prayer before reading, matching the synagogue blessing recorded by Maimonides, to which the people answer Amen.
Henry makes the verse the pattern of coming to the word — Ezra the people's mouth to God, the people joining in Amen, lifted hands, and bowed heads of reverence and subjection.
Clarke hears a Christian echo, 'Glory be to God for his holy Gospel,' sealed with its Amen.

outliers.note: Observes that 'the great God' is the narrator Nehemiah's phrase, not necessarily Ezra's own, and that the words of the blessing are nowhere reported.

themes: worship with faces to the ground

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch take the named men as themselves Levites (the copula a clerical slip), several recurring in Neh. 9:4, their office being to instruct by expounding the law.

Wesley reads the instruction as both translation of the Hebrew into the common Chaldee/Syriac and exposition of God's mind applied to the people, and 'in their place' of the several stations for hearing, each with its own scaffold.
Gill takes the listed men and the Levites as of one teaching order.
Henry sees the Levites dispersed to teach those beyond Ezra's hearing, a mercy of ministers apt to teach (Mal. 2:7), the hearers composed each in his place.

Keil and Delitzsch reject the Rabbinic 'translation' sense for a paraphrastic exposition and application of the law; Ellicott reads 'gave the sense' and 'caused to understand' as one — they expounded, naturally translating into vernacular Aramaic, as they read.

Wesley holds they gave both a Chaldee translation and an exposition; Clarke, seeing here the seed of preaching from a text, distinguishes four movements — read the law, read distinctly, gave the sense (put weight to it), caused them to understand.
Henry draws the rule that teachers must explain and give the sense, for expounding joins reading and preaching, making the one intelligible and the other convincing.
Gill: Ezra read and expounded, relieved by others when weary.

debates.question: What does 'read distinctly / gave the sense' mean — translation or exposition?

sides.position: It included rendering the Hebrew into the vernacular Chaldee/Aramaic alongside exposition
Not a translation by fixed rules but a paraphrastic exposition and application of the law

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch trace the weeping to convicting portions of Deuteronomy read on the holy new moon; Ellicott notes high festival was unfit for public sorrow, the day of atonement and covenant-fast being the fit occasions.

Henry reads law and gospel together — the law works terror and the tender tears were good, yet unseasonable on a feast, for sorrow for sin must not hinder joy in God; Nehemiah enters here to still the weeping.
Clarke: the Tirshatha is Nehemiah by office; the holy day is for rejoicing in the God who turned their captivity and restored the law.
Gill identifies the Tirshatha as the governor, an office held by Zerubbabel and now Nehemiah.

themes: the people weep at the law
mourn not on a holy day

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch fix the 'fat' as fat meat and the 'sweet' as sweet drink (Isa. 25:6), the 'portions' as food-gifts to the poor (Esth. 9:22; 1 Sam. 1:4), folding the needy into the joy; Ellicott renders the great sentence 'delight in Jehovah is a strong refuge.'

Clarke enlarges the charity and calls religious joy, tempered by dependence on God, a means of strengthening the soul, a continual feast and medicine; Wesley: cheerful, thankful service gives strength for duty and against enemies.
Henry: this holy joy, not carnal mirth, is strength — for the feast's duties, oil to obedience, and armour against the tempter.
Gill hears the governor bid the people go and enjoy the day.

themes: eat the fat and drink the sweet
the joy of the LORD is your strength

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch render the Levites' appeal to give over weeping, for the day is holy; Ellicott notes Ezra's word relayed by the Levites in every direction against an almost irrepressible emotion.
Gill: the Levites made the people quiet and easy, backed by the governor's authority.

themes: hold your peace, the day is holy

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch: the address had its effect, the people going off to festal repasts because they took the words to heart; Ellicott: 'had understood' means they caught the meaning of the command to rejoice and obeyed.

Henry marks the order of the affections — passion soon restrained when unseasonable, holy mourning making way for holy mirth — and grounds the joy in understanding the word, Bibles and ministers being the joy of God's Israel.
Gill: they went their way to eat and drink freely and cheerfully.

themes: the sweetness of the word grasped

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch note the heads of houses, priests, and Levites gathering to Ezra to take attentive interest in the law; Ellicott: not the multitude but the chiefs, come to consider the almost forgotten festival, the dwelling in booths having fallen into disuse.
Wesley honours the Levites who confessed ignorance rather than feign knowledge, more careful to learn their duty than keep their reputation.
Henry: unwearied appetite for the word (the more we converse with it, the more we covet it), and the teachers now sitting as learners at Ezra's feet (Ezra 7:25) — for teachers must first be taught.
Gill sets the day as the second of the month, after the law had been read and explained.
Keil and Delitzsch insist the precept was not deliberately sought beforehand but met with in the course of reading, and so moved them to keep the feast in booths and publish the proclamation.
Clarke fixes the feast of tabernacles as commemorating the wilderness sojourn after Egypt, now the peculiar duty of a people just delivered from Babylon.
Gill: they perceived the feast of tabernacles enjoined in the law (Lev. 23:34).
Henry: diligent searchers find things forgotten; the feast, a memorial of tent-life and a type of gospel joy, foretells the nations' conversion (Zech. 14:16).

Keil and Delitzsch set out the full proclamation to fetch olive, pine, myrtle, palm, and thick branches to make booths; Ellicott, finding no such command in Leviticus, adopts Houbigant's emendation 'when they heard it, they proclaimed,' the branches gathered as circumstances allowed.
Gill reads the verse with Jarchi's supplied sense of publishing the call abroad.
Wesley identifies the Mount of Olives, planted with such trees for the city's use in this very feast, as put by eminence for any place near the cities of Judah.

debates.question: How should the 'saying' that introduces the proclamation be read?

sides.position: As the written precept straightforwardly published (with the branches named)
Emended with Houbigant to 'when they heard it, they proclaimed,' there being no such command in Leviticus, the branches such as circumstances allowed

themes: adapting the letter of the law

schools.summary: Ellicott distributes the booths through the whole city — roofs, inner courtyards, the courts of the house of God (made by the temple's ministers), and the streets and open spaces near the gates where strangers built.
Clarke pauses over the flat Eastern roofs, everyday places of rest and sleep, now turned festal by the booths set on them.
Gill pictures the people going out to the nearby mountains to fetch the branches for their shelters.

themes: booths on roofs and in courts
the city as a wilderness camp
the whole city obeying the word

schools.summary: Ellicott hears pathos in 'the children of the captivity' and is careful that though the feast had been kept before (1 Kings 8; Ezra 3:4), it had never been kept thus, with the whole people dwelling in booths.

Wesley reads 'done so' of manner and joy — never so joyfully or so religiously, the law now read every day, not only the first and last; Clarke: none since Joshua so heartily celebrated, and dismisses the Maccabean sacred-fire legend as unworthy of credit.
Gill: all the returned came up to Jerusalem, where alone the feast was kept.

outliers.note: Dismisses the legend, told in the books of the Maccabees, of a sacred fire hidden in a well and rekindled on the altar, as worthy of no credit.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch leave the reader unnamed and note the daily reading was ordered only for the sabbatical year (Deut. 31:10), fixing the last day as the seventh, the eighth being a separate solemn assembly (Lev. 23:36); Ellicott reads 'according unto the manner' of that Azereth (Lev. 23:36).
Gill takes Ezra as the reader who went through the law day by day, though only the first and last days were the holy convocations.

Henry praises perseverance in the word through every day, the eighth-day assembly closing the feast on the twenty-second, yet the twenty-fourth kept for fasting — joy and godly sorrow each holy in its season.

themes: seven days and the eighth assembly
joy giving way to the fast
